principles.text: Stance unchanged from the 7/22 flip: fully bearish/short. Not many tradable ideas this morning, but 'we're getting a small bounce — which could favor the short side': in a downtrend a bounce is supply, an entry opportunity for shorts, not a reason to cover.

Never size up after a losing streak to make the losses back as fast as possible — that instinct (his own, 2-3 years ago) is the first step of a vicious cycle that ends in a larger drawdown. After yesterday's string of stop-outs he explicitly kept size flat and did not 'keep shorting every bounce regardless of the risk or the market.'

Your original idea can be right and your execution decent and you can still lose: a lot of the time price does not follow your expectations, or knocks you out before going your way (MARA stopping him out and then breaking down). That, not bad analysis, is much of what makes trading difficult.

Intraday-short patience rule learned from yesterday's losses: don't take the FIRST 5-minute reversal at the open — that's how he kept stopping out in the first 15 minutes. Waiting for a later, cleaner reversal (WULF today) caught the strong follow-through with none of the churn.

Rotation read on the bounce day: defensive sectors leading, midcaps leading, tech getting beaten down, many names selling off hard into resistance after the open — a risk-off tape beneath a green-ish index, consistent with staying short.

Leader character change as short timing: SNDK surfed the 50 EMA for the entire uptrend; now it is losing the 50 for the FIRST time and bouncing into the declining 50 — the first such bounce after a long trend is the highest-quality short entry ('shorting yesterday would be the best timing'). Whether it now surfs the 50 DOWN, 'no one knows — we will see.'

This correction may be more destructive than people expect, precisely because the post-liberation-day rally taught everyone that buying every dip prints money. Habits and mindsets formed in a lockout/stage-2 rally (2020-21 analog: Tesla, EV names, speculative garbage later sliced in half) get people smashed when the market deteriorates: 'in a very strong uptrend a lot of mistakes would be forgiven... when the market starts to slow down, you're gonna lose all the money back. Buy the dips — until it doesn't.'

Late-stage crowding marker: before April the heat on SK Hynix wasn't crazy, but on this last leg up retail piled into the semi leader with leverage, margin, even loans — the crowd arrives in the last part of the rally. 'There will be another SK Hynix in the future and we'll see the same thing again' — the ticker changes, the story doesn't.

Bear-market playbook from his own 2022 (+4–8%): drastically reduce trade count; accept that shorts learned in a bull market mostly fail at first (nearly all his 2022 shorts lost); most of the year's return can come from ONE well-trailed trend trade (long BOIL). Survival plus one trend carried the year.

Parabolic-extension exit (from Qullamaggie, on his 2022 BOIL trade): when a position accelerates ~17% above the daily 9 EMA, you don't have to wait for the first close below the daily 9/10 — selling into strength is fine, or downshift and trail the 60-minute 9/10 EMA so the lower timeframe takes you out near the top.

Filter the noise by demanding PROOF: he anchored on Qullamaggie's style because Qullamaggie is a verified example of the strategy working at the highest level, while most strategies online (99%-win-rate MACD/RSI/Bollinger 'secret indicator' videos) come with no proof — just a Patreon link and a discount code.
Verify everything with the market: 'everybody could be wrong, but the market is always right.' Even mentors' rules are hypotheses to test against your own fills, not gospel.

How his signature entry was born: reviewing 2023-24 losers he found breakouts/opening-range-high entries stopping him out and THEN going his direction, with rising frequency. Once you find 5-10-20 examples of the same failure, redesign the entry — wait for the shakeout and buy the intraday pullback / 5-minute range breakout reversal instead of the opening-range high. Takeaway: don't blindly follow the standard entry; let your own losing-trade review re-engineer the trigger.

Knowing vs understanding an entry: the tight-range breakout isn't 'the best buy point' because a book says so — it's best because it strictly limits downside and precedes range expansion (high win rate, 10-20R potential). Once you understand the FUNDAMENTALS (defined risk + win rate + reward), the same logic can justify buying a 21-EMA pullback — breakout vs pullback are opposite tactics built on identical reasons.

Keep asking why about every detail in the market (why did Tesla find resistance THERE?). Most of the time you won't find the answer — but the observations you eventually generate yourself are the most valuable thing you own, 'because that originates from you, not the others,' and what you truly understand works far better than what you copy.

Discretionary vs systematic is a personality fit, not a ranking: he sides with the 'art of trading' and keeps no checklist/rulebook, but a trader with a strong ego, emotional swings, or weak self-discipline may be better served by hard rules. 'There is no one way of trading — which one suits you the best?'

The best lessons are always in the drawdowns, the mistakes, the difficult periods, the market crashes (to a viewer who lost 80% overtrading options) — and living through one mania (this AI run, which 'will definitely fade away one day') is what saves your fortune in the NEXT one, decades later.

Into a pivotal event week (FOMC + mega-cap earnings): the events can't be predicted, so sizing is a self-knowledge question — if a 10% gap against you would trigger revenge trading or panic selling, cut exposure BEFORE the event; if you can genuinely handle the volatility, managing positions as usual is not wrong. He trades the chart, not the news/macro — 'the chart would let me know.'

Aggression is earned, twice over: he can flip from heavily long at Wednesday's open to 6-7 short positions by Thursday only because (1) a triple-digit YTD profit cushion absorbs the risk — 'if I'm not up triple digits right now, probably I'm not opening six or seven short positions in one day' — and (2) he's gotten better at throttling down during losing streaks. Without both, the same flip is just overtrading toward a large drawdown; 'you don't have to trade like this.'

Trading the short side as well as the long keeps you from becoming over-bullish in uptrends/sideways markets and helps you spot weakness earlier. The cost: getting chopped in trendless tape and sometimes turning too bearish during a normal base — but the benefits outweigh the disadvantages.

Aggressive sizing is only an edge when done CORRECTLY — in hindsight the winners look like front-running, but the same behavior failing produces a large drawdown. Reward always comes from risk; the job is maximizing return while actively managing the drawdown — 'and it's not easy. I definitely got lucky this year.' He also says he does not really use volume on lower timeframes (114:29).
